paragraphs: 1 When Jacob learned that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, “Why are you staring at one another?”
2 “Look,” he added, “I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.”
3 So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt. 4 But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers, for he said, “I am afraid that harm might befall him.”
5 So the sons of Israel were among those who came to buy grain, since the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan.

6 Now Joseph was the ruler of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all its people. So when his brothers arrived, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground. 7 And when Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them. “Where have you come from?” he asked.
“From the land of Canaan,” they replied. “We are here to buy food.”
8 Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him. 9 Joseph remembered his dreams about them and said, “You are spies! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
10 “Not so, my lord,” they replied. “Your servants have come to buy food. 11 We are all sons of one man. Your servants are honest men, not spies.”
12 “No,” he told them. “You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
13 But they answered, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more.”

14 Then Joseph declared, “Just as I said, you are spies! 15 And this is how you will be tested: As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here. 16 Send one of your number to get your brother; the rest of you will be confined so that the truth of your words may be tested. If they are untrue, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!”

17 So Joseph imprisoned them for three days, 18 and on the third day he said to them, “I fear God. So do this and you will live: 19 If you are honest, leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households. 20 Then bring your youngest brother to me so that your words can be verified, that you may not die.”

21 Then they said to one another, “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
22 And Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must account for his blood!”

23 They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them. 24 And he turned away from them and wept. When he turned back and spoke to them, he took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.

context_lines: The famine reaches Jacob's household in Canaan. Hearing that grain is available in Egypt, he sends ten sons to buy food but keeps Benjamin at home because he fears harm may come to him. The brothers arrive among other buyers and bow before Joseph, the ruler responsible for selling grain.

Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. He remembers his dreams and treats them as strangers, accusing them of spying out the country's weakness. They insist that they are honest men from one family, explaining that the youngest brother remains with their father and another is no more. The reader knows that the brother they describe as gone is standing before them.

Joseph initially proposes sending one brother for Benjamin while the others remain confined. After three days, he changes the arrangement: one will stay, while the rest may carry grain home and return with the youngest brother to verify their account. He states that he fears God and allows food to be taken to their hungry households.

Under this pressure, the brothers speak about what they did to Joseph. They remember his distress and their refusal to hear his pleas, and they connect their present trouble with that guilt. Reuben recalls his warning against harming him. They do not realize Joseph understands because he has been speaking through an interpreter.

Joseph turns away and weeps, then returns and has Simeon bound before them. His hidden emotion shows that the encounter reaches him deeply. The family is confronting its past, but Joseph has not yet disclosed his identity, and the test involving Benjamin remains ahead.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read the encounter as a turning point in the brothers' awareness of their guilt and the beginning of a movement toward reunion. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 42:9, 21](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) understand Joseph as testing them with repentance in view. Wesley also criticizes Joseph's appeal to Pharaoh's life; his reading does not treat every part of Joseph's conduct as beyond criticism.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 7:11–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) directly recalls the famine, the first journey for grain, and Joseph making himself known on a later visit. The brother rejected by the family has become the person able to preserve it. Their bowing also recalls the future they once tried to prevent when they rejected his dreams.

The family's preservation includes a confrontation with its wrongdoing. [2 Corinthians 7:9–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/7.htm) later distinguishes sorrow that produces repentance from sorrow alone. Here the brothers acknowledge what they did; the following events will show whether changed actions accompany that acknowledgment. Their story allows us to see reconciliation developing through truth and responsibility as well as the provision of food.
